problem: Prior object-navigation work targets any instance of a category in single rooms, and standard inputs (images, 2D maps) or naive GNNs cannot represent relational goals or scale to large multi-room scenes with many irrelevant objects.
motivation: Realistic household tasks need a specific instance defined by hierarchical relations (object-furniture-room), e.g. 'apple on the table in the kitchen'. This requires compact memory that captures relations, and large scene graphs (~100 nodes) dilute useful information under naive pooling.
key_idea: Build an incremental scene graph, encode it with a heterogeneous graph transformer, and pool node embeddings with a task-driven attention that keeps only nodes whose semantic category appears in the goal description, all trained end-to-end with PPO.
insight: Naively adding scene graphs or metric maps as memory does not help in large scenes (Task 3 SR: SG 0.458 and RGB-D+MM 0.554, versus RGB-D only 0.586); goal-conditioned attention pooling is what makes the graph useful (SR 0.879). With distractors in Task 2, SR drops from 0.967 (no attention) to 0.425 and is restored to 0.900 by attention. Pre-mapping furniture into the graph adds further gains, and learned attention can match task-driven attention but needs longer training.
method: Incremental scene graph: nodes are objects and rooms (semantic class, pose, size in agent frame); directed edges are relations (onTop, inRoom, roomConnected); built from a perfect simulator detector and accumulated over steps.
HGT encoder: three Heterogeneous Graph Transformer layers with ReLU, using per-edge-type matrices in attention.
Task-driven attention pooling: weighted mean over node embeddings with weight 1 for nodes whose category matches any category in the goal, else 0.
Multimodal fusion: RGB-D via 3 conv layers + FC, one-hot goal via 3 FC, graph feature concatenated and passed through 3 FC layers.
PPO policy: RLlib PPO, 8 parallel envs, ~1.5M steps, separate 3-layer FC policy and value heads; geodesic-distance shaping reward plus success (+10) and wrong-object (-5) rewards.
Pre-mapping variant (PM): the graph is initialized with all furniture and rooms, excluding the target object.

setting.backbone: HGT scene-graph encoder + CNN RGB-D encoder + MLPs, PPO (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: RL interaction in simulation, ~1.5M environment steps per experiment (about 1M to converge on Task 3); one iGibson scene (Wainscott_0_int), plus an eight-scene appendix experiment
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + one-hot goal (object-relation-furniture-room) + incrementally built scene graph
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: forward 0.2 m, backward 0.2 m, turn left/right 30°, stop
setting.privileged: Ground-truth perfect object detector and semantic/room labels used to build the scene graph; the PM variants additionally get a pre-mapped furniture graph

numbers.extra: incremental scene graph, no pre-mapping; averaged over 20 episodes and 3 seeds; GT detector
pre-mapped furniture scene graph given at episode start

numbers_note: All benchmarks are the authors' own new HRON tasks (not standard benchmarks); SR/SPL are printed as fractions 0-1 and copied as printed. Training curves are only in figures.
results: On the large-scene Task 3, the attention model reaches SR 0.879 / SPL 0.577, versus 0.586 for RGB-D only, 0.554 for the metric-map variant, 0.458 for SG without attention, 0.423 for the GCN baseline and 0.095 for the Yang et al. baseline. Pre-mapping raises it to 0.921 SR. With distractors, attention is essential (Task 2: 0.900 vs 0.425 SR).
limitations: Scene graphs are built from a perfect simulator detector rather than raw perception.
Attention is a hand-designed goal-category indicator, which is a strong prior.
Navigation only, with no manipulation or dynamic scenes; evaluation is mainly in one iGibson scene, with a limited-scale multi-scene study.
compares_to: Yang et al. visual navigation with scene priors
